title: self-esteem and self-compassion
subtitle: two ways of relating to ourselves

steps.prompt: what does the negativity bias do to a day?
steps.answer: it makes one hard moment loom larger than the good ones. noticing the good moments helps them count.

steps.text: self-esteem is how highly we rate ourselves. it often rises after wins and dips after setbacks.
how does that match everyday life?

options.label: it goes up and down with how things go
options.reply: that's what the research describes, too. it tends to follow results.

options.label: it feels fairly steady
options.reply: good. that can be a real strength.

options.label: depends on the day
options.reply: that makes sense. most of us are some of each.

steps.text: in a large survey study, self-compassion was linked with steadier feelings of self-worth than self-esteem was, and with less comparing to other people.
self-compassion has three parts: kindness toward ourselves, knowing other people struggle too, and noticing a feeling without being swept away.

steps.prompt: try each on, and notice which has more room in it:
lines: i have to get this right to be okay.
i want to get this right, and i'm okay either way.
steps.reply: no score here. the second leaves a little room for a rough day.

steps.text: in four experiments, people encouraged to be self-compassionate about a failure were more willing to put in extra effort to improve afterward.
so self-compassion isn't lowering the bar. it can sit beside caring a lot.

steps.prompt: which of these feels like a small act of self-compassion? pick any to keep:
options: i can want more and still be on my own side.
i can be gentle and still care about this.

steps.text: self-esteem tends to follow how things go. self-compassion is a steadier way of treating ourselves, and it doesn't seem to cost motivation.
steps.evidence: moderate (surveys and experiments; links, not proof of cause)

steps.text: once today, when something doesn't go as hoped, ask: what would i say to a friend about this?

grounding.idea: self-compassion was linked with steadier self-worth and less social comparison than self-esteem
self-compassion after a failure increased motivation to improve
